Which "Kind" of Players are Most Likely to Contribute a Large Amount of Data to PLAICraft?

Introduction:

PLAICraft is a free version of Minecraft developed by PLAI lab at UBC. The PLAI lab needs users to interact with the game so that they can collect data on user/game interactions and then use this data to train advanced AI (embodied AI).

My project aims to help answer the broad question #2 "We would like to know which "kinds" of players are most likely to contribute a large amount of data so that we can target those players in our recruiting efforts."

I am looking into this question specifically by asking "Can number of hours played predict the gender of the player?".

A greater number of hours played indicates that the player is contributing larger amounts of data. By seeing if there is a correlation between higher number of hours played and gender, this would help with locating target audiences to advertise the game to and in turn increase player hours.

The data set used was the Players Data Set: This data set is a list of all game players and data for each player.

  • Number of Observations:196 (individual players)
  • Number of Variables:7

Variables of the Players Data Set:

  1. Experience
  • Categorical Ordinal (character in R)
  • The players experience level playing Minecraft
  • Veteran (Been here since the old days. (Before 2015)
  • Pro (I am an experienced and pro Minecraft player)
  • Regular (I regularly play Minecraft)
  • Amateur (I’ve played a few hours on Minecraft)
  • Beginner (completely new to Minecraft)
  1. Subscriber:
  • Categorical Nominal
  • True if subscribed to game related emails
  • False if not
  1. HashedEmail:
  • Categorical Nominal
  • Email address transformed to a fixed number of characters for a unique ID per player
  1. Played_hours:
  • Numerical Continuous
  • Total hours played
  1. Name:
  • Categorical Nominal
  • Male
  • Female
  • Non-binary
  • Prefer not to say
  • Two spirited
  • Agender
  • Other
  1. Age:
  • Numerical Discrete (integer in R)
  • Age (7 to 99)

library(tidyverse)
library(repr)
library(tidymodels)
options(repr.matrix.max.rows = 6)
## load required models into R for analysis 

set.seed(5)
## set seed once, ensures consistent randomization each time/reproducibility of randomization. 

## read the players data set into R. 
players<-read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rchicoin/dsciproject/refs/heads/main/players%20(2).csv")
##players

# convert the gender categoring to a factor for analysis 
players<- players |>
    mutate(gender = as_factor(gender))
players

##Mean of hours played
playersMean<-select(players, played_hours) |>
map_df(mean, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(playersMean)<- c("Mean of hours played")
playersMean

##Median of hours played 
playersMedian<-select(players, played_hours) |>
map_df( median, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(playersMedian)<- c("Median of hours played")
playersMedian

## Standard Deviation of hours played
playersStandardDeviation<-select(players, played_hours) |>
map_df(sd, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(playersStandardDeviation)<- c("Standard Deviation of hours played")
playersStandardDeviation

##Minimum value of hours played
playersMin<-select(players, played_hours) |>
map_df(min, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(playersMin)<- c("Minimum value of hours played")
playersMin

##Maximum of hours played
playersMax<-select(players, played_hours) |>
map_df(max, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(playersMax)<- c("Maximum of hours played")
playersMax

## This is a table showing the count of each type of gender 
players_gender_count<-select(players, gender)|>
    group_by(gender)|>
    summarize(n())
colnames(players_gender_count)<-c("gender", "count")
print(players_gender_count)

## this is a bar chart for a visualization of the table above. 
players_gender_chart<-players_gender_count|> ggplot(aes(x = gender, y = count)) +
geom_bar(stat="identity")+
    xlab("Gender") +
    ylab("Number of Players") +
    ggtitle("The Number of Players by Gender")
players_gender_chart

##I made this chart to see if there is a trend between male and female subscribers, to see if this trend would support/align with the player hours trend"

geom_bar(stat= "count", position = "dodge") +

    ylab("Number of Players") +
    labs(fill = "Gender") +

## remove "prefer not to say" because it is like "n/a"
players<- filter(players, gender!="Prefer not to say")
players

#split data into training and testing data 
players_split<- initial_split(players, prop = 0.75, strata = gender)
gender_train <- training(players_split)
gender_test<- testing(players_split)

## create recipe with gender subtraining data, step and scale data, although only using one predictor so not super necessary 
gender_recipe<- recipe(gender ~ played_hours, data = gender_train)|>
    step_scale(all_predictors())|>
    step_center(all_predictors())

## create model
knn_spec<-nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular", neighbors= tune())|>
    set_engine("kknn")|>
    set_mode("classification")

# choose number of folds for cross validation 
gender_vfold<- vfold_cv(gender_train, v= 5, strata = gender)

## create tibble with possible values of k 
k_vals <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from = 1, to = 100, by = 5))

## fit the knn model 
knn_results<- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(gender_recipe)|>
    add_model(knn_spec)|>
    tune_grid(resamples = gender_vfold, grid = k_vals)|>
    collect_metrics()

## show results for all k values based on accuracy 
best_k<- knn_results|>
    filter(.metric =="accuracy")
best_k

## find the max values for accuracy using different values of K 
knn_results_max_mean<- select(knn_results, neighbors, mean)|>
                    arrange(desc(mean))

knn_results_max_mean

## plot the accuracy values vs different values of K. 
accuracy_plot<- ggplot(best_k, aes(x= neighbors, y = mean)) +
    geom_point()+
    geom_line()+
    labs(x = "Neighbors", y = "Accuracy Estimate")+
    ggtitle("Accuracy vs Number of KNN Chosen")
accuracy_plot


## Since 26/31/36 are all max values and the model has consistent ~ approx 65% accuracy starting at 26, we will use 31 as our K to prevent the
## significant drop off seen to the left of 26 (using k = 21) 

## Begin evaluating on the test set
gender_recipe_new<- recipe(gender ~ played_hours, data = gender_train)|>
    step_scale(all_predictors())|>
    step_center(all_predictors())

## create model with the best nearest neighbor value 
knn_spec_new <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular", neighbors = 31)|>
    set_engine("kknn")|>
    set_mode("classification")


## create workflow with new recipe and predictors 
knn_fit<-workflow()|>
    add_recipe(gender_recipe_new)|>
    add_model(knn_spec_new)|>
    fit(data = gender_train)

knn_fit

# fit the gender test data 
gender_test_predictions<-predict(knn_fit, gender_test)|>
    bind_cols(gender_test)

# assess the accuracy of the predictor 
gender_test_predictions|>
metrics(truth = gender, estimate = .pred_class)|>
filter(.metric == "accuracy")

## figure out how the genders are ordered in order to assess precision of each. 
gender_test_predictions|>pull(gender)|> levels()

Discussion:

I found that using hours played does not result in being able to predict the gender of the player very well. This resulted in approximately 65% accuracy, 70% precision, and 30% recall.

I somewhat expected this to happen because there are a few outliers in the data where there are a few females who played for a large amount of hours. The data was also unbalanced, there are more males in the data set than any other gender. I think it is interesting because there is usually a bias that men would be more likely to play video games for many hours, however some of the players with the most hours are female. It could be interesting to figure why/how these women got into playing video games. It could be interesting to figure out how to figure out how to market the game to this demographic of women and see if they could get more of these players to be aware that PLAICRaft exists and therefore increase PLAICrafts user hours.
